g.text: DS18B20 - the 1-Wire protocol engine on both sides
reset, presence, 0xCC, 0xBE, two read bytes; LSB first, sampled INSIDE the slot
FIRMWARE SIDE - firmware/ds18b20.pe
CLAIM
PINOE = 0x00, TXPIN = OW_DATA, PINOE = OW_DATA
1-Wire idles HIGH, and the idle state is the pull-up
RESET
the host's pulse
TXPIN = 0x00 - the line goes LOW
dmem[12] = 0 (the delay's return phase)
COARSE pair (4,40), OW_RST = 58: 485.5 us
A COUNTED DELAY, because nothing on the wire
says when 480 us is up
PH0
release, then settle
PINOE = 0x00 - RELEASE, the sensor may pull low
dmem[12] = 1
FINE pair (2,13) from here on: one outer step
is 69 clocks = 1.22 us, which is what a 5 us
slot needs
OW_T15 = 14, a 15 us settle
PH1
wait for the PRESENCE
spin until LOW, then spin until HIGH.
BOTH edges are waited for, with no counted 15 us
between them - the pulse's length is the
sensor's to choose (60-240 us) and the host
cannot know it. If no sensor is there the first
loop never exits, which is correct for a bus
with no timeout in this ISA.
WRITE A BIT
LSB first, no shifting
the bit to send is the byte's own BIT 0, so
the loop needs no shift: read the byte, mask
bit 0, send, SHR the byte so the next bit 0 is
the next bit of the frame.
dmem[6] holds the byte to send, dmem[2] the
bits left. EIGHT slots per byte.
THE WRITE PATH MUST CLAIM THE PIN.
1-Wire writes DRIVE: release-then-set-the-level
does not pull the line down, and the pin is
RELEASED at ph0, so TXPIN = 0 alone would leave
the line HIGH and the sensor would see a 1 for
every bit. The model caught this - it decoded 0
write bits because the line never went low.
short low, then release
PINOE = OW_DATA, TXPIN = 0x00
OW_T5 = 5: 5 us of low, the datasheet's 1-15 us
then PH2, which RELEASES and waits
OW_T55 = 49: the rest of the slot, ~55 us
hold low for the WHOLE slot
PINOE = OW_DATA, TXPIN = 0x00, and it
STAYS: the phase goes to 3, not to 2
OW_T65 = 57: 65 us, the datasheet's ~60 us
then PH3 releases and the next slot starts high
PH5
the byte is sent
SHR the byte, dmem[2]--, more bits?
dmem[7]-- : 2 then 1 then 0. After the decrement,
0 means BOTH 0xCC and 0xBE are out.
THE DELAY AND THE PROTOCOL MUST HAVE DISJOINT
dmem OWNERSHIP. This counter was on dmem[10],
which is the DELAY ROUTINE's middle-counter
TARGET - so every delay overwrote it and the
byte transition read whatever the delay left
behind. A shared slot between them is not a
warning, it is a lost phase transition.
READ A BIT
the hybrid wait
the host INITIATES: PINOE = OW_DATA,
TXPIN = 0x00 - a 6 us initiation pulse, because
the SENSOR presents the bit as a LEVEL held
across a known instant.
OW_T40 = 23: a fixed 25.4 us wait, then
A previous version SPUN for the sensor's own
falling edge here, and it raced the model's
transitions: the line was still low from the
initiation, so the loop exited at once and every
sample landed a whole slot early. Counting to a
fixed instant cannot race.
PH4
SAMPLE THE LEVEL
IN A, PIN; AND A, OW_DATA
JNZ rb_was_zero
RELEASED (high) is a ZERO on the wire;
PULLED DOWN (low) is a ONE - the OPPOSITE of a
write slot, where the host pulling the line down
IS the zero. The first version read the
opposite and both bytes came back EXACTLY
complemented: 0x2b as 0xd4 and 0x01 as 0xfe.
then SHR the accumulator with the new bit at the
TOP, so the FIRST bit read slides down to bit0 by
the eighth: 1-Wire is LSB first.
DLY1/DLY2/DLY3
the delay
TWO pairs:
(4,40) 511 clocks = 8.5 us a step - the reset
(2,13) 69 clocks = 1.22 us a step - the slots
A DISPATCH IS A FUNCTION OVER EVERY PHASE THE
PROGRAM USES. dmem[12] carries the phase and a
subtract chain picks the return address, because
the ISA cannot return to seven addresses. Two
bugs lived in this chain, both from patching one
dispatch for two different loops: it first handled
0-3 and sent everything >= 4 to ph4, which
dropped a write-1's high period into the read path;
and when the read loop was given phases 4 and 5
it collided with the write loop's 4 and 5.
PARK
done
dmem[14] = 1 - both bytes are in. THE TB'S
OBSERVABLE, so "hung mid-byte" (0) and
"finished" (1) are different failures.
TXPIN = 0x00, then JMP halt: no HALT in the ISA.
PH2
PH3
SENSOR SIDE - tb/tb_pe_soc_ds18b20.v
WATCH
the model is written FROM THE DATASHEET,
not from the firmware - which is why it was
right when the firmware was wrong
it drives tRDV at the datasheet's MAXIMUM
(15 us), so "sampled too early" is falsifiable
and its read edges come off the PADS rather than
off its own state, which is what stopped it
losing the master's next release while still
inside the previous bit's hold
RESET + PRESENCE
host low >= 480 us, then the sensor
pulls low for 60-240 us and releases
COMMANDS
0xCC SKIP ROM, then 0xBE READ SCRATCHPAD,
LSB first, eight slots each, and both are
DECODED FROM THE WIRE
SCRATCHPAD
sixteen read slots, the model's own
decode, and the firmware's two banked bytes
CHECK
what is claimed
1. the reset pulse is > 480 us
2. the presence pulse is inside 60..240 us
AND the host's pin_oe is released on every
clock of it
3. every WRITE slot's low period is inside its
own band (1-15 us for a 1, 60-120 for a 0)
4. exactly 16 read slots
5. every read slot's initiation pulse is inside
6. the SAMPLE INSTANT is inside the sensor's
data window with >= 2 us of margin at BOTH
ends
7. dmem[0..1] == 2b 01, LSB first
Why the polarity is different in the two directions,
and why the two cannot share one sample idiom.
In a 1-Wire READ slot a ONE is the line LOW: the
slave holds it down for the rest of the slot. In a
WRITE slot it is the other way about, because there
the host is the one pulling down. The read path
first borrowed the write path's sample test, and
both bytes came back exactly complemented.
A sensor that transmits its data inverted still
transmits DATA. Both bytes still had eight bits and
a plausible number of ones. Nothing in the run looks
wrong until the bytes are compared - which is why the
way to tell a polarity bug from a protocol bug is to
look at the ACCUMULATOR, not the waveform.
Why the read is "wait, then count to a fixed instant"
and not "wait for an edge".
The obvious version spins for the sensor's own falling
edge. It races: the line is still LOW from the host's
own initiation pulse, so the loop exits at once and
every sample lands a whole slot early. The version
that works is release, wait 25.4 us, SAMPLE THE LEVEL -
which is the DHT11 lesson applied the other way round.
There, the host had to synchronise because the sensor's
bit PERIOD varies. Here the host has to count because
the sensor's bit VALUE is a LEVEL, and a level read at a
fixed instant needs no edge at all.
Why the open-drain bit is deliberately NOT set.
pe_pinmux has an OD bit and this is the open-drain
case, so leaving it clear looks like an omission. It
is a decision, and it costs something: with OD set, a
pin holding 1 RELEASES rather than drives high, so
with OD set a pin holding 1 READS BACK AS RELEASED -
a write of 1 and a write of 0 look identical on the
pin, and the edge-wait loops cannot see the sensor's
pulses at all.
OD buys nothing here and costs the one thing the pin
read-back is for. The i2c_pins.pe idiom - "write out=1
or out=0 and never touch oe or od again" - is right
for a bus where the LEVEL IS THE DATA. 1-Wire is the
opposite case: the data is a TIME and the level is
just a carrier for it.
presence found
bit 0 set
bit 0 clear
dmem[12] == 2, a 1's low is over
dmem[12] == 5, the 55 us are over
more bits, or the next byte
dmem[12] == 3, a 0's slot is over
the byte is sent
dmem[7] hit 0: BOTH commands are out
dmem[12] == 4, the sample instant
dmem[3] != 0, or the next byte
dmem[8] hit 0
